title: Peripheral Perfusion Trend — Deteriorating Circulation
scenario: A 24-year-old client is admitted with a long-leg cast applied four hours ago after a tibial fracture. The nurse performs serial neurovascular checks on the casted leg and records the findings.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical
questions.stem: What does the trend in the neurovascular flowsheet most likely indicate?

options.text: Worsening perfusion to the extremity, consistent with developing compartment syndrome
Normal postoperative swelling that will resolve on its own
Improving circulation as the cast settles
An expected response to elevation of the limb

questions.rationale: Progressively delayed capillary refill, a weakening then absent pedal pulse, cooling and dusky toes, escalating pain, and new numbness all show deteriorating perfusion — the classic picture of acute compartment syndrome, a limb-threatening emergency.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical
questions.stem: Based on the 15:00 findings, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Position the extremity at the level of the heart, not elevated above it
Prepare for possible cast removal or bivalving
Elevate the leg well above heart level and apply ice
Reassess in two hours before taking further action

questions.rationale: Absent perfusion is an emergency: notify the provider, keep the limb at heart level to preserve arterial flow, and anticipate relieving the constriction. Elevating above the heart reduces arterial supply and delaying reassessment risks permanent tissue loss.
